analysis.one_liner: Makes the repeal of the federal estate tax on inherited wealth permanent.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 195 House cosponsors but never received a vote: after referral to the Ways and Means Committee on its first day, no committee or floor action followed before the Congress ended in early 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2001 tax law phased out the federal estate tax, but only temporarily: the repeal was scheduled to expire after 2010, when the tax would return. This bill removed that expiration date, making the estate tax repeal permanent. The Ways and Means Committee never acted on it, so no vote was ever held.
analysis.who_benefits: The heirs of the largest estates. Under the 2001 law as written, by 2009 the estate tax applied only to estates larger than $3.5 million per person ($7 million per couple), meaning the tax already touched only a small fraction of the wealthiest families; making the repeal permanent would permanently free those families' heirs from the tax.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the 2001 tax law to strike the sunset provision that applied to its estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer tax provisions, making the repeal of the estate tax permanent [S2].
The bill text exempts the estate tax title from the section 901 sunset, so that the repeal would continue beyond 2010 [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally. The estate tax raises tens of billions of dollars a year, almost all of it from very large estates; making the repeal permanent removes that revenue permanently, which must be made up through borrowing, other taxes, or reduced federal spending.

drawbacks.text: Making the repeal permanent would permanently eliminate a federal revenue source that, under the phase-in schedule then in effect, fell only on estates above roughly $3.5 million per person, concentrating its benefits on the heirs of the wealthiest families [S2].

The revenue loss is recurring rather than one-time: because the bill strikes the sunset provision itself, the lost estate tax revenue continues indefinitely, adding to deficits or requiring offsetting taxes or spending cuts [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are large but narrowly concentrated: the heirs of the very largest estates, a small fraction of families. The costs are diffuse: every federal taxpayer shares the burden of permanently lost revenue through larger deficits or other taxes. The bill offers no offsetting revenue provision, so an honest supporter would acknowledge it is a pure revenue loss targeted at the top of the wealth distribution.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 7, 2003, the opening day of the 108th Congress [S5].

It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day, and the action history shows no further action — no committee vote, no floor vote, no further referral — through the end of the Congress on January 3, 2005 [S5].
It nonetheless attracted 195 cosponsors, 182 Republicans and 13 Democrats [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never became law, the estate tax repeal did not become permanent in this Congress, and the federal government retained a revenue source that falls only on the largest estates. The main beneficiaries of the bill's failure are general taxpayers' fiscal position, narrowly understood; the concentrated interest it would have served — heirs of the wealthiest estates — did not get what it sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal taxpayers; the wealthiest estates' repeal push failed.

for.name: Jennifer Dunn
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 195 cosponsors on the first day of the Congress [S1].

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Bill Thomas (R-CA)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no markup, no vote, no report — leaving it to die at the end of the Congress [S5].

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Republican: 182 of 229 House Republicans cosponsored, compared with 13 of 205 House Democrats [S4].

industries.note: The bill would permanently exempt the largest estates from the federal estate tax. Under the 2001 law's schedule, only estates above roughly $3.5 million per person paid any tax, so the benefit concentrates in the top fraction of a percent of families, while the lost revenue is borne by everyone through deficits or other taxes.

industries.industry: Estate planning attorneys and wealth advisers
industries.note: Permanent repeal would eliminate the estate tax exposure that drives much of high-net-worth estate planning work. Their interest in keeping the tax on the books runs alongside the public's interest in the revenue it raises.
